chunks: And from him (Al-Hassan ibn Mahbub) from Al-Abbas ibn Ma'ruf from Hammad from Hariz from Zurarah from Abu Ja'far and Abu Abdillah (peace be upon them both) that they said:

The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) excused (exempted from khums/zakat) the khudur (fresh vegetables). I asked, 'What is the khudur?' They said, 'Everything that does not have longevity: vegetables, watermelon, fruits, and similar things that spoil quickly.' Zurarah said, 'I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'Is there anything (due) in the sugarcane?' He said, 'No.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on zakat or khums for fresh vegetables and perishable produce in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that 'khudur' refers to perishable goods like vegetables, melons, and fruits which are exempt from zakat due to their rapid spoilage. The dialogue with Zurarah further specifies that sugarcane (qasab) is included in this exemption, highlighting the juristic principle of removing hardship from owners of short-lived assets. This ruling underscores the Shia legal focus on practicality, ensuring that temporary, non-storable produce does not become a financial burden through obligatory alms-tax.
